scenes.lower: The North Indian Ocean from space, 17 May 2023, painted with that day's satellite sea surface temperature
scenes.say: Satellites see the ocean every day. Only the top: its temperature, salt, winds. What lies underneath, they cannot see. That is where the heat is.
This is Satelight.
In the next few minutes, we will go over what we built, how it works, what it is useful for, and how accurate it is. You can follow along with the timestamps below.

scenes.quote: The objective is to estimate the three-dimensional ocean temperature using only surface satellite observations.
scenes.cite: SIH 2026 · PS 26066 · INCOIS, Ministry of Earth Sciences
scenes.say: INCOIS asked for the ocean's temperature in three dimensions, using only what satellites see at the surface.

scenes.lower: Bay of Bengal, 17 May 2023 · the sea peeled away, surface to 1,000 m · satellites only
scenes.say: This is the Bay of Bengal. Let's go down. Sunlight fades by 200 metres, and no satellite sees below that. Satelight keeps going, level by level, to a thousand metres, from the surface alone.

lines: Sea surface temperature|OSTIA, block-averaged to the grid
Sea surface salinity|SMOS and SMAP, multi-observation product
Sea level and its anomaly|DUACS, 0.25°: the common grid
Surface currents, east and north|OSCAR, NASA PO.DAAC
Surface winds, east and north|CCMP, four synoptic times averaged to the day
scenes.say: It reads eight things satellites measure every day: sea surface temperature, salinity, sea level and its anomaly, and the currents and winds, in both directions. All put on one common grid.

lines: Trained on GLORYS12, 2010 to 2020. GLORYS is the target, never an input.
scenes.say: An encoder squeezes each point's surface into 32 numbers: the embedding. A decoder turns it into temperature at the 15 standard depths, and blanks out anything below the seabed. It learned from GLORYS, 2010 to 2020, never taking it in.

scenes.lower: 24 September 2026 · INCOIS's fishing zones, each with how deep the warm water goes
scenes.say: For fishermen. INCOIS already tells them where fish are likely to gather, every day. We add how deep the warm water goes in each of those zones, from the latest satellite day.

lines: Periyamangodu, North Tamil Nadu: warm water to about 115 m, mixed layer 20 m, on 24 September 2026.
Nine coastal languages across INCOIS's fourteen sectors. Machine-translated, labelled so, and read aloud by the browser's own voice.
scenes.say: பெரியமாங்கோடு: சுமார் 115 மீட்டர் ஆழம் வரை வெதுவெதுப்பான நீர், கலப்பு அடுக்கு 20 மீட்டர்.

scenes.heading: How deep the warm water goes, error against Argo
lines: The depth of the 20 °C isotherm, the core of the thermocline, from each profile's 15 levels
scenes.say: Against held-out floats in the Bay of Bengal, climatology misses that depth by 19.3 metres, Satelight by 13.7, and GLORYS by 12.0. On average, it puts it 9.2 metres too deep.

scenes.lower: Cyclone Mocha, 6 to 17 May 2023 · heat above 26 °C · IMD's best track
scenes.say: For forecasters. A cyclone feeds on heat stored in water above 26 degrees. We map that fuel every day. Follow Cyclone Mocha up the Bay, and watch the fuel drain behind it.

lines: Tropical cyclone heat potential: the heat above 26 °C, from each profile's 15 levels
scenes.say: Against the floats, climatology misses that heat by 21.0 kilojoules per square centimetre, Satelight by 12.9, and GLORYS by 11.9. In the Bay of Bengal, Satelight matches GLORYS.

scenes.lower: Now: 24 September 2026 · four satellite fields · no reanalysis covers this day yet
scenes.say: GLORYS arrives months late. Satelight only needs what the satellites have already sent. Press Now, and you see the ocean of the twenty-fourth of September, 2026. Days ago, not months.

lines: Four fields reach 24 September: SST, salinity, sea level and its anomaly. Currents and winds are 30 days behind, so all eight reach 30 August.
scenes.say: Measured today: sea level arrives the same day, temperature a day late, salinity six days late. GLORYS is 99 days behind.

Against the real-time floats of those three months, four fields beat climatology to 150 metres, in the whole box and the Bay, but only to 75 in the Arabian Sea. All eight, a month late, reach 200 metres in both seas.

scenes.lower: 15 November 1997 · the whole North Indian Ocean · labelled a comparison
scenes.say: It works backwards too. This is November 1997: the whole North Indian Ocean, rebuilt at every depth, from satellites that were already watching.

lines: Argo profiles per year in 45–105°E, 5–30°N, from the Argo GDAC profile index.
scenes.say: From 1993 to 2000, not a single Argo float surfaced in this box. But the satellites saw every day.
We tested it on 2005 to 2009, years before anything it trained on. It beats climatology at every depth, in both seas, and stays behind GLORYS down to 500 metres.

scenes.lower: Bay of Bengal, 15 March 2023 · magenta: a heatwave 50–150 m down, under a normal surface
scenes.say: Some heatwaves hide below the surface, 50 to 150 metres down, under a sea that looks normal from space. Magenta marks where Satelight finds them.

lines: The 50–150 m layer above its 90th percentile for the day and place, the surface not (Hobday et al. 2016, applied to a layer). One day per float.
scenes.say: Against the floats, Satelight catches 182 of the 336 hidden layers they found. Its skill is 0.31, GLORYS reaches 0.49. It also over-flags, 484 false alarms, which fits its warm thermocline.

scenes.lower: Mixed-layer depth, 15 July 2023 · where a hull sonar's surface duct ends
scenes.say: The sonar layer: the depth of the mixed layer, where a hull sonar's surface duct ends. This one isn't there yet. Over the whole box it misses by 15.4 metres, climatology by 14.4, GLORYS by 11.5.

scenes.lower: One held-out Argo float against every model, with its QC flag, data mode and source file
scenes.say: Click a float, and it is checked against every model. Floats from 2023 and 2024, never seen in training, each with its quality flag, data mode and file.

Climatology is the floor, GLORYS the ceiling. Satelight beats climatology down to 300 metres, in both seas, and stays behind GLORYS, which already took in these floats. The thermocline is hardest, and runs warm.

lines: unet-abs's embedding, its first three components as colour, 15 July 2023: water that looks alike to the model, painted alike.
scenes.say: The embedding is saved every day, as a file. One encoder's embedding predicts the mixed-layer depth, never trained on, better than the raw inputs: R squared 0.351 against 0.255. No single one also sorts the seasons. That proof is half met.
Every number in this video comes from one harness we built. Anyone can run it again with one command.

lines: The embedding proof|half met: a second encoder is next
The thermocline|runs warm: +0.88 °C at 100 m against the floats, where GLORYS runs +0.67
The sonar layer|no better than climatology yet, except in the Bay of Bengal
The translations|machine-made: each needs a native speaker's check
scenes.say: What is not done yet: the embedding proof, a warm thermocline, the sonar layer, and translations that need a native speaker's check. Each one is written down.
That is Satelight. Everything, every number included, is at the link on screen.
